turns.user: How should Simandou affect Capesize tonne-miles and rates in 2026–27? I keep seeing 120 million tonnes a year.
turns.answer:
The 120 Mt/yr figure is the combined nameplate export capacity of the shared rail–port system (SimFer blocks 3&4 at 60 Mtpa plus WCS blocks 1&2 at 60 Mtpa), not a 2026–27 run rate. First ore shipped in December 2025; SimFer reported only 2.2 Mt shipped in H1 2026, and Breakwave Advisors estimated roughly 16 Mt for full-year 2026. Rio Tinto guides a 30-month ramp-up to SimFer's 60 Mtpa after rail commissioning (Q1 2026), which points to ~2028–29, with the full 120 Mtpa generally expected around 2029–30 (Drewry, Nov 2025).

On tonne-miles, the direction is unambiguous. Morebaya–Qingdao is roughly 11,000 nm, about three times the Australia–China distance and close to the Brazil C3 route, so each tonne shifted from the Pilbara roughly triples tonne-miles. Drewry estimates 120 Mt on Guinea–China would absorb ~180 Capesizes versus ~64 for the same volume from Australia. The net effect depends on substitution: displacing Australian ore adds tonne-miles, displacing Brazilian ore is closer to neutral, and displacing Chinese domestic ore adds seaborne demand. Wood Mackenzie (April 2026) expects Simandou to be the largest driver of seaborne supply growth, displacing higher-cost supply.

For 2026–27 rates, the effect is supportive but diluted, for two reasons:

- **Volume is still small.** Single-digit-to-~20 Mt/yr against a ~1.5 Bt seaborne iron ore market cannot move the market on its own. Broker Ifchor Galbraiths (May 2026) credited Simandou with underpinning the spring 2026 bulker rally, but that was one factor among several.
- **The trade is being structured off the spot market.** SSY data cited by Splash (August 2026) shows VLOCs over 220,000 dwt took nearly half of H1 2026 Simandou shipments, and Chinese-controlled tonnage is ~40% of the VLOC orderbook. Winning International's 325,000 dwt WinningMax vessels are purpose-built for the trade, and China Merchants' Ming Wah subsidiary has fixed long-term tonnage to the China Mineral Resources Group supply chain. If VLOC ordering continues at the 2024–25 pace, much of the incremental demand may never reach the conventional Capesize spot market (Banchero Costa, via Splash).

For context, the Baltic Capesize Index is 6,400 as of 9 September 2026 (OilPriceAPI reprint of Baltic Exchange data). The structural tonne-mile story is real; the 2026–27 spot-rate payoff depends on how much of it is absorbed by dedicated Chinese VLOC capacity before it reaches the open market.

turns.user: Is Simandou already inside today’s $55k Cape 5TC, or is that a 2027 story?
turns.answer:
Short answer: the $55k 5TC is a 2026 print, but Simandou iron ore is not yet inside it in any material volume sense. The current strength is an Atlantic story — Brazilian iron ore, Guinean bauxite, and coal — with Simandou's physical contribution still negligible.

What is actually in today's print (Week 36, data to 4–7 September 2026):

- C5TC closed the week at $54,791/day on 4 September, the highest since 21 October 2021 (Xclusiv weekly, citing Baltic data); the Baltic Week 36 report put the BCI 182 5TC above $58,000/day, and Hellenic's weekly analysis shows average C5TC at ~$53,508/day, +$8,612 week-on-week.
- The rally's stated drivers: Brazilian iron ore exports up ~20% week-on-week, Guinean bauxite exports ~55% higher year-on-year on a four-week rolling basis, Q2 2026 Capesize tonne-miles +4.9% YoY (iron ore +2%, bauxite +7.7%, coal +15.3%), and unfixed Capesizes ballasting to the South Atlantic roughly halved year-on-year. C3 Tubarão–Qingdao hit a multi-year high of $41.55/mt, ~70% above its September 2025 average. Weather disruption in the Pacific tightened prompt tonnage on top of that.

Where Simandou fits:

- Volumes are still tiny: SimFer shipped 2.2 Mt in H1 2026, and Breakwave Advisors estimated ~16 Mt for full-year 2026. That cannot move a 5TC print.
- Its current role is indirect — part of the West Africa loading complex on C3, and part of the tonne-mile narrative that is keeping forward pricing firm (September/October FFAs around $50,000/day, Q1 2027 near $32,000/day, unusually firm for a seasonally weak quarter).
- The physical Simandou effect on the 5TC is a 2027+ story, and even then it may be diluted: SSY data cited by Splash shows VLOCs over 220,000 dwt took nearly half of H1 2026 Simandou shipments, and Chinese-controlled tonnage is ~40% of the VLOC orderbook. A large share of the ramp-up volume is being structured onto dedicated Chinese VLOCs (WinningMax, Ming Wah/CMES) rather than the conventional spot Capesize market that the 5TC measures.

So: the $55k is real and current, but it is not a Simandou number. Simandou is a 2027–29 tonne-mile story whose spot-market payoff depends on how much of the volume stays off the conveyor belt.

turns.user: People say Guinea bauxite is the real Atlantic Cape story. How does that sit next to Simandou?
turns.answer:
The claim is correct for the current market: bauxite is the live Atlantic Capesize story, and Simandou iron ore is the future one. They are two legs of the same Guinea-to-China long-haul complex, run by the same Chinese-linked consortia, and they increasingly compete for the same logistics capacity.

**Bauxite is the now story.** Guinea exported roughly 183 Mt of bauxite in 2025, up about 25% year-on-year (Breakwave Advisors, March 2026), and H1 2026 exports rose a further 15% to a record (Reuters via Mining Weekly, July 2026). Guinea is ~70% of global seaborne bauxite, and the trade is the second-largest Capesize commodity after iron ore, at roughly 12,000 nm to China. DNV puts bauxite at ~16% of Capesize tonne-mile demand in 2025, equivalent to ~250 additional vessels versus 2015. In the current rally, Xclusiv's Week 36 report cites Guinean bauxite exports up ~55% year-on-year on a four-week rolling basis and bauxite tonne-miles +7.7% in Q2 2026 — that is a material part of the Atlantic tightness behind the $55k 5TC.

**Simandou is the next leg of the same machine.** The bauxite chain was the template: Winning International built the SMB bauxite operation with barges, floating cranes and transshipment, becoming the world's largest bauxite shipper, and then applied the same model to Simandou — the Trans-Guinean railway, Morebaya, and the WinningMax VLOC fleet (gCaptain profile, November 2025). Breakwave's framing is useful: Guinea bauxite on Capesizes is around 160–180 Mt/yr and plateauing, and with Simandou the country becomes a ~300 Mt/yr Capesize exporter — effectively "another Brazil to China route" (Brazil ~380 Mt/yr).

**But the two trades also cannibalize each other.** The clearest evidence is Ifchor Galbraiths' July 2026 note: Guinea bauxite loadings slumped to 1.3 Mt/week, down 50% week-on-week and 38% year-on-year, as Winning shifted transhipment capacity to Simandou. The floating transshipment units and the controlled Chinese fleet are shared between the two commodities, so Simandou's ramp-up does not simply add a new demand layer on top of bauxite — it reallocates the same physical and commercial infrastructure. That is also why both trades pass through to the conventional spot Capesize market only partially: bauxite has long run on Winning's own tonnage, and Simandou is being structured onto dedicated VLOCs (SSY data: VLOCs took nearly half of H1 2026 Simandou shipments).

**Caveats on the bauxite leg.** Growth is not guaranteed: Breakwave notes delivered economics into China are tightening as freight on the route moved from the mid-$20s to above $30/mt, and the Guinean government has been considering an export cap amid oversupply (Hellenic, May 2026). Signal Ocean also flags that Guinea's planned alumina refining capacity could divert ~14 Mt of bauxite from seaborne markets by 2030.

Net: bauxite is what is actually tightening the Atlantic today; Simandou is the structural tonne-mile story for 2027–29. The analytical risk is double-counting — they share geography, owners, transshipment assets and controlled tonnage, so the combined ~300 Mt Guinea story is not simply additive for the spot Capesize market.
